newsitem.title: USA: Clinton proposes $138 billion in Medicare savings.
newsitem.headline: Clinton proposes $138 billion in Medicare savings.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday offered a concession to the Republicans in an effort to forge a balanced budget agreement, proposing $138 billion in savings over six years in the Medicare health care programme.

The surprise announcement, one day after Clinton's inauguration for a second term, appeared designed to make good on his promises to reach out to the Republicans who control Congress to break the long-standing logjam on the budget.

"I am going to do my best to reach out to the Republicans," Clinton said before a budget strategy meeting with advisers. "I want to meet them halfway on this and on many other issues and I hope they will meet me halfway."

He added: "I am determined that if we will do that, we can resolve our remaining differences and reach agreement to balance the budget and do a lot of other good things for the American people as well."
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, one of Clinton's key Republican critics on the budget, said he was encouraged by what he called his "realistic" Medicare savings estimate.

"I am encouraged that the president has presented a more realistic estimate of the savings needed to make the Medicare programme solvent for the next decade," the Mississippi Republican said in a statement. "We will certainly examine this budget proposal carefully so that we can begin to move toward a common solution to the crisis faced by the possible bankruptcy of the Medicare system."

Clinton and his aides described the $138 billion figure as a step that is both literally and figuratively halfway toward the Republicans' position on Medicare, the popular and politically sensitive health care programme for the elderly.

They said the figure compared to the $116 billion in savings over six years that Clinton proposed last year, as calculated by the Congressional Budget Office, and the $158 billion that the Republicans had put forward.

Medicare is a politically delicate subject because of the president's success in hurting Republicans during last year's election for their efforts to rein in the programme, a tactic the Republicans called "Mediscare."
Clinton rejected that term on Tuesday and repeated that he wants to work with the Republicans.
